name: Whitening LED tray with red light

lead: These trays combine a whitening gel with LED lights, some red, and are sold for home use. The light is marketed as speeding up whitening.
Research on light in professional bleaching is mixed, and no trial of red-light trays specifically was found.

paras: The gel's peroxide breaks down stain molecules. The light is claimed to accelerate this, though reviews of light activation disagree on whether it adds benefit and note possible heating.
Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported effects. Whitening results can fade within months, and peroxide limits differ by country.

lead: A whitening LED tray with red light is a consumer device that combines a mouth tray, usually loaded with a peroxide-based or other whitening gel, with built-in light-emitting diodes, some of which emit red light, marketed for at-home tooth whitening. The light component is sold as a way to speed up or enhance the action of the gel.

Tooth whitening generally works by breaking down pigment molecules with peroxide, and in-office systems have long paired gels with halogen, LED or plasma-arc lights [1]. Published reviews of that light-activation practice have reported mixed results: one meta-analysis found light could help when used properly, while a later study found no improvement and noted possible heating of tissue [1]. No published clinical trial specific to red-light LED trays was located for this article.
infobox: At-home whitening tray with LED light
Peroxide limits vary by region (e.g. EU retail 0.1% hydrogen peroxide; FDA-endorsed gels up to 6% hydrogen peroxide or 16% carbamide peroxide)[1]

paras: Products in this category pair a mouthpiece with a battery-powered LED array, often advertised with blue and red wavelengths, and a whitening gel. Manufacturers describe the light as an accelerator or as a way to make treatment more comfortable. Specifications differ widely between brands and product claims are made by sellers rather than by regulators.

Hydrogen peroxide, delivered directly or released from carbamide peroxide, produces free radicals that break coloured molecules into smaller, less visible fragments [1]. Tray-based systems with carbamide peroxide are reported to give roughly one to two shades of improvement, sometimes visible within about three days [1].

In professional settings, light-accelerated bleaching uses halogen, LED or plasma lights with high-concentration gels for roughly 6 to 15 minutes [1]. A 2012 systematic review by He and colleagues is described as finding that light can increase results without extra sensitivity when used properly, but can raise sensitivity and offer no added benefit at high peroxide concentrations [1]. A 2015 study by Baroudi and Hassan found no improvement from light activators and noted a risk of raised tissue temperature [1]. Whether red wavelengths specifically add anything beyond the gel has not been established in sources reviewed for this article.

The most common adverse effect of whitening is tooth sensitivity, reported in a majority of people in some in-office studies, and gum irritation can occur when trays fit poorly [1]. Dental bodies generally advise examination before whitening and caution in pregnancy, children, active decay or gum disease [1].
No studies found. Related research on light-activated in-office bleaching exists and has produced mixed findings [1].

lore.intro: Red-light whitening claims circulate mainly in product marketing and social media; no forum material was available for this entry.

claims.claim: Red or LED light makes whitening gel work faster or better
